newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - French single currency efforts get EU boost.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French single currency efforts get EU boost.

text.p: France's efforts to qualify for European monetary union received a major boost on Thursday when the European Commission said it accepted a controversial plan to use pension funds to cut the budget deficit in 1997.

The head of the Commission's statistics office Eurostat cleared the plan to transfer 37.5 billion francs ($7.35 billion) from state-owned France Telecom to the budget, despite reports that German, British and Dutch experts had opposed the move.
Eurostat Director General Yves Franchet was responsible for the technical assessment of whether the French plan was in line with agreed European Union accounting rules.
"This does indeed qualify as a capital transfer which means they are in the clear," Commission spokesman Patrick Child told reporters.

The announcement came only two days after reports that an advisory European Union advisory accounting committee had not been able to approve the payment, causing the franc to fall against the German mark on currency markets.

At issue was whether the transfer of money to cover future pension liabilities could be used by the French government in its accounting to reduce its 1997 deficit to meet one of the Maastricht treaty criteria for monetary union in 1999.
France sees the transfer as vital in cutting its deficit to the target of three percent of gross domestic product.

EU officials estimate that the transfer will help reduce the French deficit by between 0.4 and 0.5 percent of GDP. In return the government will assume the state-owned telephone operator's pension liabilities.

Critics have said the one-off transfer smacked of creative accounting and ran counter to guidelines in the Maastricht treaty for countries to take sustainable economic measures to qualify for the single currency.

Sources said earlier this week that a number of committees organised by Eurostat had been discussing the issue but that they had been unable to agree on France's plan and a letter had been sent to EU member states asking for their opinion.
Child said a "small minority" of the representatives of member states and of the national central banks had "expressed doubts about the approach proposed by the French."
He did not name the sceptical countries, but an EU source said on Wednesday that German, British and Dutch officials had argued against allowing France to use the transfer.
The conclusion that Eurostat's Franchet had drawn from the consultations was that "a large majority of participants were able to accept the French approach," Child said.
Asked whether other EU countries struggling to meet the single currency criteria could do similar accounting exercises, Child said all cases would be examined on their merits.
"Clearly there is no discrimination between member states, all countries are affected equally by the rules."
"So in identical circumstances in another country it would seem to me logical that the same result would be achieved," Child added.
Various countries have been accused by economists of window-dressing to cut budget deficits in 1997, the year on which eligibility for membership will be judged.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer has warned that one-off measures by European nations to reduce budget deficits would not be enough to allow them to join a single currency.

In an interview in French daily Le Monde earlier this month, Tietmayer declined to say which countries would join in 1999, but said Italy, which plans a special one-off euro tax to reduce its budget deficit in time to qualify, would be welcome -- provided it could keep up its efforts afterwards.
($=5.1 francs)
